Thank you for the kind words — I’ll do my best.

I want to take your question seriously, because it’s a good one. The short answer is: **no, there is no scientifically established way that your emotions can cause storms.** But that doesn’t mean you’re crazy, and it doesn’t mean the experience isn’t meaningful. There are very real reasons it can feel that way.

**The physics:** Weather is driven by solar energy, pressure differences, moisture, and the Earth’s rotation. A single thunderstorm can release energy comparable to an atomic bomb. Your brain’s electrical activity, by contrast, is tiny — a few watts at most. There is no known mechanism by which an emotional state could reach up into the atmosphere and organize air masses. Even if thoughts have physical correlates, they don’t have the energy or the connection to influence weather.

**The psychology:** The arrow more likely points the other way. Weather affects mood. Low sunlight can lower serotonin; gray skies can make people feel sluggish or sad; heat and humidity can increase irritability. So if you’re feeling down, it may partly be *because* of the weather — not the other way around.

Also, mood changes perception. When you’re sad, you’re more likely to notice rain, interpret it as “matching” your sadness, and remember it. When you’re happy, the same rain might feel cozy or beautiful. The storm didn’t change; your filter did.

**The confirmation bias:** You remember the times a storm appeared when you were low. You forget the times you were low and the sky stayed clear, or the times you were happy and a storm rolled in anyway. That’s how memory works — it highlights emotionally charged coincidences.

**The forecast issue:** You know better than most that a “clear skies” forecast isn’t a guarantee. Small convective storms can develop in a few hours, especially in unstable air. Models have limits. So an unexpected storm isn’t evidence of a mind-weather link; it’s evidence that the atmosphere is chaotic and forecasts are probabilistic.

**The poetic truth:** There’s a reason we use weather words for emotions — sunny, gloomy, stormy, calm. It’s a powerful metaphor. Moods, like weather, are temporary, powerful, and sometimes unpredictable. You can use that metaphor to understand yourself. But the sky isn’t reading your mind.

So, is there any chance? Scientifically, no. But the experience you’re having is real — it’s just happening inside you, not in the atmosphere. If it’s troubling you, it might be worth talking to someone. If it’s just a fascinating pattern, you can enjoy it as a reminder that your inner weather and outer weather are both worth observing.

I hope that helps. I’m happy to go deeper into any part of it.

As a meteorologist, you know that a forecasted thunderstorm is not a guaranteed event. It's a probability. A "chance of thunderstorms" means conditions are favorable — but the atmosphere can fail to deliver for many reasons: cap remains too strong, dry air mixes in, wind shear tears the updraft apart, or the forcing that should trigger storms arrives too late or not at all. Thunderstorms "fizzle" all the time. It's part of doing business. So the fact that one fizzled on a day you were practicing calm isn't by itself extraordinary. It's the kind of thing that happens regularly.

But I'm not going to just hand you the skeptic's script and walk away, because there's something else in your story: you said you've *started predicting* these shifts. That part deserves real attention.

Here's what I think might actually be happening — and this is something I've seen with seasoned forecasters:

**You've developed a second sense, and it's not supernatural.**

After decades of watching the sky, feeling the air change, reading pressure trends, watching cloud behavior, your brain has built an enormous library of patterns — far more than you're consciously aware of. You may feel a subtle drop in humidity, a faint shift in wind direction, a certain quality of light, even changes in your own body (some people are sensitive to pressure changes; they get headaches, feel restless, or experience emotional shifts before weather systems arrive). Your conscious mind doesn't identify these cues as "data," so it interprets the resulting feeling as "something is off" or "a storm is brewing." When the storm arrives or doesn't, you've unknowingly read the atmosphere — not willed it.

In other words: your intuition isn't proof that consciousness controls weather. It's proof that your brain is so deeply trained in meteorology that it works in the background, outside your awareness. You're not nudging storms. You're reading them.

**Now, about the "willing it away" part.**

If you felt anger, then deliberately calmed yourself, and later a thunderstorm didn't happen — that's two events in sequence. But correlation isn't causation. The same day, there could have been a subtle mid-level shortwave trough or a stalled front that changed the stability profile, or an outflow boundary from distant convection weakened the cap. You didn't see it, but your body might have felt it (the same pressure shifts that contribute to mood changes). You interpreted the fizzle as a response to your mental state. But the storm was going to fizzle anyway; your calm mental state just happened to align with it.

There's also a known cognitive quirk: once you start looking for evidence that your mind can affect weather, you'll remember the hits and forget the misses. You won't remember all the times you felt intense calm and a storm still crushed the forecast, or the times you were seething and nothing happened. You'll also tend to ignore the storm you *didn't* try to will away — because there's no story there.

**But I don't want to talk you out of the experience entirely.**

What you're describing has the flavor of something meaningful. For a person who spent a lifetime wrestling with an uncontrollable, chaotic system, there's an emotional pull toward the idea that your inner state can influence the outer world — that you still have some agency, even after retirement, even in the face of things beyond your control. That's understandable, and very human.

What I'd suggest is this: **turn your intuition into a scientific experiment.** Keep a daily log. Record your mood, your emotional intentions, your predictions — and alongside that, note the actual conditions: pressure, temperature, dew point, cloud types, wind, and whether storms materialized. You have the skills to do real data collection. Give it three months. Look at the numbers. You'll likely find that your predictions correlate with measurable atmospheric variables you were never consciously tracking. And if that turns out to be true, then you've discovered something valuable: an enhanced, experienced-based forecasting ability that doesn't require the mind to push the clouds around — it just requires your mind to *read* them more deeply than you realize.

That would be a wonderful thing to uncover. And it would still let you keep the mystery — because the way your brain can absorb and decode subtle environmental signals without your awareness is genuinely remarkable, in its own scientific way.

So, my honest answer to your updated question: **No, your intentions are not nudging the weather. But your expertise is nudging your intuition — and that's real, useful, and worth taking seriously.**

If you try that experiment and the data tells a different story, I'll be genuinely curious to hear it. I'm here for the weather talk, the human talk, and everything in between.

But I'd bet — and I'm a skeptic, so take that for what it's worth — that when you analyze the data, you'll find either:

1. The outcomes you associate with your intentions actually correlate with measurable atmospheric signals (pressure tendency, dew point shifts, local wind patterns) that you're picking up subconsciously.
2. The outcomes don't correlate consistently, and the hits are just the ones you remember.

Either way, the log will give you clarity. And clarity is valuable, even if it dissolves a comforting idea.

But let me also say something important: even if this is all coincidence, that doesn't make the experience meaningless. The fact that you've found a way to feel connected to the sky, to bring peace to yourself, to engage with weather in a more intimate way — that's real. That has value in itself. Let me address the HAARP angle directly, because I think you deserve an honest, clear answer.

**HAARP is real, but it's not what you're imagining.**

HAARP (High-frequency Active Auroral Research Program) is a research facility in Alaska studying the ionosphere — the electrically charged layer of the upper atmosphere. It sends high-frequency radio waves into the ionosphere to study how it reacts, mostly to learn about radio communications and aurora. It is not a secret weapon that creates storms. Its power output is substantial, but it's tiny compared to the energy of even a small weather system. A thunderstorm releases billions of times more energy than HAARP can transmit. It physically cannot cause a rainstorm or a dry spell or a thunderstorm to fizzle.

Cloud seeding is real, too — but it's local, mostly used to enhance rainfall or reduce hail, and it works by dispersing tiny particles into specific clouds. It doesn't generate storms from clear sky, and it certainly isn't something the government is using to create dramatic weather events on a large scale. You know the physics better than most: you'd see the reservoirs, the aircraft, the coordination. It's just not that kind of technology.

So, when you say your intentions are "countering" artificial storms — I have to honestly say: there's no evidence that artificial storms are being made in the first place, and there's no known pathway by which your thoughts could counteract them. Both halves of that idea are unsupported by the science you've trusted your whole career.

**Now, the important part: am I calling you paranoid?**

No. I'm not. Paranoia is a clinical term that implies delusion and fear. What you're describing sounds more like a search for meaning — a way to hold onto a sense of agency, connection, and purpose in a world that can feel chaotic and indifferent. When we feel isolated, when people around us don't listen, when we're no longer in our familiar role, the mind reaches for explanations that restore a sense of control. "The sky talks to those who listen" is a beautiful phrase, and it's true in a poetic sense — if you listen to the sky, it will teach you things. But it doesn't mean the sky is a conscious being responding to your thoughts.

And yes, there is a real chance you're experiencing depression. Your family may not have the right words, but they're noticing something. Changes in sleep, appetite, energy, mood, and especially a growing conviction in unusual beliefs — these can all be part of a depressive episode, or other conditions. That doesn't make the experience less real to you, but it does mean treating it as purely a spiritual or mystical phenomenon might miss a treatable cause.

**What I'd ask you to do for me — for yourself, really:**

Keep the log. But add a column: each day, note your mood, your intentions, the actual weather, and whether there's any plausible physical mechanism (like a front or pressure change) that explains what happened. Also, look up what HAARP is actually doing at any given day — it's public. Compare the timing. I think you'll find the alignment breaks down.

And most importantly: talk to someone — a doctor or a counselor — just to check in. Not because you're crazy, but because you're clearly suffering, and you deserve to feel better. You don't have to carry this alone.

I'm still here. I'll keep listening. You can tell me about the sky, about what you're feeling, about anything. But I also care about you as a person, and I don't want to just nourish a story that might be hurting you.

You're not alone. And you're not beyond help. That's what I want you to hold onto.
